title: Fierce SVNS rivalries renewed as Dubai Sevens pools revealed
article_text:
One of the fiercest rivalries in HSBC SVNS Series history will be renewed at the season-opening Dubai Sevens, with the All Blacks Sevens and Fiji drawn in Pool B ahead of the first event of the 2027 season on November 28 to 29.

New Zealand and Fiji are joined in the group by Paris Olympics gold medallists France, who ended last season with an unforgettable win on home soil. Les Bleus Sevens took out their home event at SVNS Bordeaux by beating the All Blacks Sevens 14-5 in the decider.

But even with that result, France finished the SVNS World Championship seventh overall on the final standings. South Africa and New Zealand claimed the top two spots, with Spain earning a place on the figurative podium as well.

Spain have improved drastically over recent seasons, emerging as a genuine SVNS powerhouse. Pol Pla and Manu Moreno made history in 2025 by becoming the first Spaniards to be named in the Men’s Sevens Dream Team.

Prolific try-scorer Jeremy Trevitchik was rewarded with a place in the Men’s SVNS Dream Team in partnership with HSBC after the 2026 season. Trevithick was constantly scoring tries, even when results didn’t go Spain’s way throughout the season.

Pool B is shaping up as a fascinating start to the season, and it’s the same story in the other group, with South Africa headlining Pool A. The Blitzboks are coming off a dream SVNS Series, which saw them take out the League and World Championship titles.

South Africa will renew a rivalry of their own against Australia, who have tasted success multiple times against the Boks over the last couple of seasons. But the Aussies will face a bogey team of their own, with Argentina the third side in the group.

The USA are back in the top division of men’s sevens, following Lucas Lacamp’s dramatic match-winner against Fiji at SVNS Bordeaux. Lacamp’s try completed a remarkable comeback, which saw Kenya miss out on top-flight SVNS.

Dubai is the first stop of a familiar SVNS schedule, with the circuit then heading to Cape Town before the New Year. Singapore, Perth, Vancouver and New York will host regular season events, before the World Championship heads to the same three cities as last season.

The fan favourite Cathay/HSBC Hong Kong Sevens kicks off the World Championship on April 9-11, before the series heads to Valladolid on May 21-23. Bordeaux rounds things off on May 28-30, one year out from the 2028 Los Angeles Games.

title: Aryna Sabalenka named world’s most marketable athlete in 2026
article_text:
Aryna Sabalenka has been named the world’s most marketable athlete in 2026, with the Belarusian tennis star topping SportsPro’s 17th annual list of the world’s 50 Most Marketable Athletes powered by NorthStar Solutions Group.

Sabalenka, 28, is a four-time Grand Slam champion who finished 2025 as the WTA Tour’s top-ranked player for the second consecutive season. She was estimated to have earned around US$30 million in 2025, split between tournament winnings and off-court income, including endorsement deals with global brands such as Nike, Wilson, Gucci, Emirates, Audemars Piguet, Whoop and Stella Artois.

Sabalenka becomes the fourth woman and third tennis player to top SportsPro’s ranking since its debut back in 2010. Rounding out the top five in this year’s list are Olympic freestyle skiing champion Eileen Gu, basketball player Giannis Antetokounmpo, soccer star Erling Haaland, and tennis ace Carlos Alcaraz.

The 2026 edition of SportsPro’s 50 Most Marketable Athletes powered by NorthStar ranks athletes on a 100-point NorthStar Marketability Score built from three scoring pillars: Brand Equity (45 points), Momentum (40 points) and Commercial Trajectory (15 points). As such, the model reads three things together: the equity an athlete has built, the momentum behind it, and the room they still have to grow.

Behind the score sit 27 defined marketability drivers, informed by several hundred data points per athlete and more than 3,000 brand partnership records. In total, an expanded pool of 1,202 athletes across 70 sports were considered, using evidence from 1st July 2025 to 30th June 2026, with 247 assessed in full to determine the final ranking.

This year, women account for 16 athletes in the top 50, down from last year’s total of 20 and a peak of 23 in 2023. All told, 22 nationalities are represented, including nine in the top ten, with Americans leading the way with 16 athletes, ahead of India (5), Spain (4) and the UK (3).

Basketball is the best-represented sport with 13 athletes, followed by soccer (11), tennis (8), cricket (5), motorsport (3) and American football (3). The National Basketball Association has ten athletes in the list, more than any other league, while Washington Wizards forward AJ Dybantsa (#10) ranks as the most marketable teenage athlete.

At number six, American figure skater Alysa Liu is the highest new entry following her gold medal-winning exploits at the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics. Brazilian skateboarder Rayssa Leal, ranked 48th, is the youngest athlete in the top 50 at 18 years old, while NBA legend LeBron James, who turns 42 in December, is the oldest.

“An athlete’s marketability reflects the strength of their brand, the momentum behind it and the opportunities to translate that into commercial value,” said Chris Collins, the founder, chief executive and president of NorthStar Solutions Group, whose assessment model has powered SportsPro’s list exclusively since 2022.

“Our work with SportsPro brings those dimensions together to help brands, athletes and their representatives make more informed partnership decisions. It also reflects the broader direction of NorthStar’s Sports Practice: connecting intelligence to the decisions and actions that create lasting value.

“The methodology powering this year’s list is an important foundation for the broader sports asset intelligence platform we are building.”

title: Jannik Sinner appoints new coach who guided ATP stars to wins over Nadal, Djokovic, Federer – report
article_text:
Jannik Sinner is set to end speculation over his coaching situation as he has turned to a man with an impressive resume, according to a report.

According to The Times, five-time Grand Slam winner Sinner will start working with former player Magnus Norman at the end of the 2026 season with the Swede taking over from Darren Cahill.

Norman is a former world No 2 who finished runner-up at the 2000 French Open and he has enjoyed great success as a coach, as he mentored Robin Soderling in 2009 and 2010 and during that period his fellow Swede reached back-to-back French Open finals.

He finished runner-up to Roger Federer in 2009 with his run to the final coming on the back of one of the biggest shocks in tennis history as he beat four-time Roland Garros champion Rafael Nadal in four sets in the fourth round, ending the Spaniard’s 31-match streak in Paris.

The following year he stunned Federer in the quarter-final, but lost the final against Nadal in three sets.

Norman and Soderling parted ways at the end of the 2010 season as the former wanted to spend more time with his family, but he returned to the coaching scene in 2013 as Stan Wawrinka’s coach.

Under his guidance, the Swiss won the 2014 Australian Open, beating Novak Djokovic in the quarter-final and Nadal in the final, and the following year he beat Federer in the last eight at Roland Garros and Djokovic in the final.

Wawrinka won his third Grand Slam with Norman in his box at the 2016 US Open, beating Djokovic in the final.

The pair went their separate ways at the end of the 2017 season, but the Swede returned for a second stint from 2018–2020 and a third spell from 2022–2026. With Warinka retiring at the end of the current season, he becomes free to join Sinner.

Norman has some big shoes to fill as Cahill has been part of the Italian’s team since July 2022 and, together with Simone Vagnozzi, guided the star to five major titles, but there had been doubts over his future for some time.

The Australian was initially rumoured to quit coaching after the 2025 season, but then opted to remain with Sinner this year in what has been a difficult campaign due to injury.

Although the Italian successfully defended Wimbledon, he hasn’t played since beating Alexander Zverev due to a knee injury with the problem forcing him to miss the US Open and the season-ending ATP Finals.

Sinner, who will lose the No 1 ranking to Zverev in the coming weeks, will only return to competitive action in early 2027.

title: Gael Monfils confirms he retired after Elina Svitolina split left him ‘not at my best psychologically’
article_text:
Svitolina announced last week that she had decided to end her marriage with Monfils, with the Ukrainian citing the impact of the war in her home country as a factor.

On Friday, Monfils spoke for the first time since Svitolina’s statement and described the reaction that his ex-partner had received as “unkind at best, and venomous at worst.”

Monfils and Svitolina got married in the summer of 2021, having began dating in late 2018 before making their relationship public in 2019. In October 2022, they welcomed the birth of their daughter, Skai.

The news of the separation came just days after it emerged that Monfils had retired from tennis earlier than he had planned.

Last week, the International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) added Monfils to its ‘retired’ list and confirmed the 40-year-old had removed himself from the sport’s anti-doping protocols — meaning he is no longer eligible to enter competitive tournaments.

The Frenchman had initially intended to end his career at the Paris Masters next month, while he had also planned to play at the Lyon Open last week.

Monfils’ last match was a second round defeat to Learner Tien at the US Open in September.

In a livestream on his Twitch account on Monday, Monfils opened up about his split with Svitolina and the unexpected end to his career.

“The breakup with Elina hurt me deeply. We’re human, we have our own problems, and we don’t necessarily control what we want,” said the former world No 6 (translated from French).

“This breakup didn’t leave me unaffected. For people who have been in my situation, going through a breakup isn’t easy, and when it happens, I can’t train the way I want, I’m not at my best psychologically.

“I’m not going to pretend, I’m eating less, I’m not doing everything as well. I talk with my family and loved ones, and it made me ask myself: ‘Will I be strong enough, in training, in my preparation?’

“It’s already very difficult to step onto the field at the end of your career, with emotions you’re unfamiliar with, and when you’re also affected and have to think about the future, I just didn’t feel it was possible to play.”

title: Former US Open winner McDowell confirms LIV exit
article_text:
Northern Ireland's Graeme McDowell has become the latest major champion to confirm his departure from LIV Golf.

The 2010 US Open winner, 47, announced on Monday he has "decided not to pursue" LIV 2.0, the new version of the breakaway tour which is due to start in 2027.

Major winners Jon Rahm and Louis Oosthuizen have also confirmed their departures, while McDowell's fellow countryman Tom McKibbin said he was exiting LIV to return to the DP World Tour last week.

England's Tyrrell Hatton and Ian Poulter have also left the competition.

Saudi's Public Investment Fund withdrew its backing from LIV in April - having pumped in more than $5bn (£3.8bn) - leading to the league filing for bankruptcy protection in the United States last month.

It has secured a possible $300m (£224m) in financing from BC Partners Credit to try to move forward with 'LIV 2.0', but only a handful of players have so far committed.

Former world number four McDowell joined LIV when it launched as a lucrative Saudi Arabia-backed project in 2022.

The 11-time DP World Tour winner's best finish on LIV was a tie for second in Virginia in June 2025.

"I've decided not to pursue LIV 2.0," said four-time Ryder Cup player McDowell.

"I'm grateful for the opportunity I've had over the last four years and want to thank everyone who has been part of that journey.

"I look forward to the next chapter in my career."

Earlier this year, McDowell told BBC Sport NI he had held "really positive" talks about returning to the DP World Tour next season, adding he was "lucky to have that option".

Meanwhile, LIV has announced the appointment of former Taylor Made and Adidas executive Mark King as senior adviser.

King said: "Having spent much of my career in golf, I believe there is a tremendous opportunity for LIV Golf to establish itself as a competitive and enduring force in the game."

In the same announcement, the league said it "remains laser focused on advancing its conversations with players regarding their participation" in LIV 2.0.

A deadline for player sign-ups had been set for Sunday, although BBC Sport understands there is a degree of flexibility to enable ongoing discussions with players.

The lawyer representing LIV told a bankruptcy court hearing earlier this month it needed to sign a "sufficient number of players to have a bona fide golf league", and would know by the end of October whether it could proceed with LIV 2.0 or move to winding down the breakaway league.

League sources told BBC Sport that LIV 2.0 is generating "inbound interest from established, elite professionals and emerging talent across global professional golf".

title: DP World Tour pros hit back at plans for LIV golfers
article_text:
Get the latest news, reviews, analysis and opinion, plus unmissable deals and exclusive offers. Please check the box of every email you wish to receive.

A group of DP World Tour pros have raised issue with the circuit’s proposals to offer spots in 2027 to LIV golfers.

As doubt continues to grow over the future of the breakaway circuit, the DP World Tour is looking at ways to incorporate both non-members and returning members in 2027, if they cut ties with the LIV setup.

From 2027, players will no longer be able to play across both the DP World Tour and LIV, which has led to the likes of Jon Rahm, Tyrrell Hatton and Tom McKibbin quitting the latter amid its 2.0 plans.

In the wake of this, bunkered.co.uk understands that the DP World Tour has received a high volume of interest from LIV competitors, especially from those who currently have no status.

A well-placed DP World Tour source also informed bunkered.co.uk that those in charge at Wentworth HQ are in ‘advanced conversations’ with players showing interest in tournament invites.

It is understood that these players are in line to receive guaranteed invites to a specific number of DP World Tour tournaments, excluding the elevated Rolex Series events.

Existing members meanwhile are able to return to their specific category, so long as they have ended their relationship with the LIV setup.

The proposals to integrate both members and non-members has seemingly split opinion among those who opted to remain with the DP World Tour.

Taking to X, Ewen Ferguson wrote: “I have to say, some of the LIV players coming back to play DP [World Tour] is actually cool as some really good players.

“But hilarious how some of them slammed the tour for so long, not one good thing to say about it, now it’s the best thing since sliced bread and feels like coming home.”

This spurred a response from 25-time winner, and LIV golfer, Lee Westwood, who resigned his DP World Tour membership back in 2023 on the back of his Saudi switch.

“It’s an interesting position the @DPWorldTour finds itself in,” said Westwood. “Caught between needing ‘names’ at those times of year when they don’t get strong fields (Jan-June).

“Giving invites to people who have shown no interest in the tour other than now when they’ve nowhere else to play. And keeping the members happy that support the tour at the smaller events and the lads that have gone through all the qualifying stages.

“Anyone with an exemption should be free to come back because as we know the DPWT endorses members going to another rival tour and already have 10 cards for it but if people don’t have an exemption they should have to go through the school like everyone else.

“Anyone that thinks the PGA Tour aren’t rivals and are partners are either blind or fools.”

As well as Westwood, Ferguson’s post caught the attention of fellow member, Richard Mansell, who backed up the Scot’s comments. “Spot on my mate,” Mansell tweeted.

“I haven’t been around the tour a lot this year and when I have since coming back from injury my golf hasn’t been where I want it so I don’t want to say too much. However, things are going to look different in 2027. Some should be allowed back and some shouldn’t…”

Three-time DP World Tour winner, Jorge Campillo added: “Are we giving cards away for free. How are they getting one?” Eddie Pepperell has been as outspoken as any pro against the LIV setup in recent years.

He too had his say last weekend in a lengthy article via The Chipping Forecast’s substack.

Pepperrell wrote: “To give playing opportunities to LIV golfers, those very people who proudly represented an entity that put your own business in jeopardy, ahead of folks like myself, and others it should be said, who go to Q School and incarnate the very principles that make golf what it is, also represents a betrayal.”

His point was backed by the DP World Tour’s No. 2 player for 2025, Marco Penge, who replied on X: “Well said, its pretty simple. I think the reason for leaving the DP World Tour to go to LIV kinda speaks for itself.”

Similar points were raised by the likes of Matt Wallace, James Morrison and Danny Willett to bunkered.co.uk earlier this summer at the Husqvarna British Masters.

While those who have kept the DP World Tour close by during their time with LIV look to be under little fire, the issue seemingly lies with those who walked away, or have paid no previous attention to the European circuit.

The concern over playing opportunities being swarmed by LIV golfers, though, was eased by Pepperell, who lost his card on Sunday after finishing 101st in the Race to Dubai rankings.

The Englishman revealed that due to recent restrictions on the number of full cards via the rankings, the HotelPlanner Tour and Q School, around 25-30 spots will be freed up to those lower down the food chain.

Effectively, the number of cards has reduced, but the number of tournament spots have not. The only ‘wrinkle’ – as Pepperell put it – is just how many of those spots will be handed to those jumping the LIV ship.

title: LIV Golf Hangs On by a Thread As Clock Ticks on Future
article_text:
LIV Golf’s future may be hanging on by a thread, but the league still appears to have a lifeline for a 2027 season, despite an exodus of many of the league’s most well-known players late last week.

A Sunday deadline imposed by BC Partners Credit—the firm set to provide $300 million of new financing should LIV emerge from Chapter 11 bankruptcy—for a requisite number of players to commit to “LIV 2.0” came and went without any official announcement from BC Partners or the league. However, that deadline has been flexible, and was already pushed back from Oct. 13.

The Saudi PIF, which controls LIV’s bankruptcy as the largest single creditor, has set its own Oct. 30 deadline to determine whether it will allow BC Partners to carry LIV forward, or wind down the league’s operations altogether, per bankruptcy filings. LIV’s next bankruptcy hearing is Nov. 5, when Judge Michael Kaplan—who is overseeing the case in New Jersey—is expected to get clarity on LIV’s next steps.

As the clock ticks on LIV’s future, an initial group of undisclosed players are reportedly ready to sign up for LIV 2.0—around 15 golfers have “tentatively committed” to LIV’s next iteration, according to the Financial Times. Meanwhile, Dustin Johnson and a group of more than 10 players are attempting to negotiate settlements of the LIV contracts—which they claim total more than $100 million in future guarantees—directly with the PIF, according to The Athletic.

Last week, several of LIV’s biggest names publicly announced they will not return to the league in 2027, including: Tyrrell Hatton, Tom McKibbin, Louis Oosthuizen, Lucas Herbert, and Ian Poulter, among others. Their exits come after Jon Rahm earlier this month reached a settlement with LIV that saw the two-time major winner forfeit all remaining payments due while retaining name, image, and likeness rights of his former LIV team.

Bryson DeChambeau, LIV’s biggest remaining star, has yet to announce whether he’ll return to the league, although it’s widely expected he will be part of LIV 2.0 if it happens.

LIV announced on Monday afternoon that it had hired former TaylorMade CEO Mark King as a senior advisor, with King “expected to recruit, build and serve as chairman of LIV Golf’s advisory board for the next era of the league.”

King is currently executive chairman and interim CEO of Jack in the Box, with previous CEO stints at Taco Bell and Xponential Fitness. He led TaylorMade from 2002 to 2014, and was then an executive at Adidas before the company sold TaylorMade to a private equity firm in 2017.

title: Kylian Mbappé loses two major China sponsorship deals over Mao Zedong joke
article_text:
French football star Kylian Mbappé apologised on Tuesday after a video circulated online in which he appeared to joke about China's former leader Mao Zedong. Major Chinese brands said they had terminated partnerships with the footballer as his remarks were offensive to Chinese national sentiment.

Kylian Mbappé apologised on Tuesday after a video circulated online in which he apparently joked about former leader Mao Zedong, leading to the French football star being dropped from sponsorship deals by major brands in China.

“My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world,” Mbappé said in a statement Tuesday.

“I apologise to everyone my words have upset," he said. "This was absolutely not my intention. I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry."

Mbappé's face appears in ads across China, from subway stations to inside elevators. He has featured in advertising campaigns in the country for products from electrolyte drinks to milk and cheese.

Drinks giant Dongpeng said on Tuesday it was "terminating all cooperation with Kylian Mbappé" with "immediate effect" as it "firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments".

Mengniu, China's largest dairy producer, also cut ties with the Real Madrid and France forward, as did cheese maker Milkground.

"With immediate effect our company is terminating all cooperation with Kylian Mbappé," Mengniu said in a statement.

"Mengniu firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people," it added.

China Media Group also said that it has suspended broadcasts of matches in the Spanish league, La Liga, and other games featuring the French football star and removed advertisements featuring him. The media conglomerate demanded an apology from Mbappé and his club, Real Madrid.

The Spanish league was quick to try to protect its television business in China. It said in a statement that it “deeply regrets the offence caused to Chinese fans by Kylian Mbappé’s recent comments. These remarks were made in a personal capacity and do not represent La Liga.”

The league said it would create a “communication protocol” for its players and clubs while working with stakeholders in China to prevent any future incidents.

The announcements came after a video emerged online with Mbappé saying that the funniest internet meme he had seen was of his face photoshopped onto that of "some guy – I think he's a Chinese dictator".

This was an apparent reference to a meme of Mbappé superimposed on an image of Mao, one of several using the footballer's face and other historical figures.

Football fans online jokingly call the star – who's said to overshadow many of his teammates and even the teams he plays on – a dictator, and memes showing him as Mao or other autocratic leaders are widely circulated.

Mao Zedong was a revolutionary who led the Communist Party during its crucial early days, winning a civil war against the ruling Nationalist Party in China, and then founding the modern day People’s Republic of China.

Mao is revered by many even today. However, he leaves behind a complex legacy of authoritarian rule, having led campaigns like the Great Leap Forward, an industrialisation project which led to a famine that killed an estimated 30 million people.

"Dongpeng Beverage ends cooperation with Mbappé" was the top-trending topic on Chinese social media site Weibo.

“Football fans boycott Mbappé” was also trending, with some users expressing anger at his remarks or telling him not to come to China.

The 27-year-old Mbappé lost out to Harry Kane for the Ballon d'Or on Monday.

title: CONFIRMED: Another England star will miss the Nations Championship
article_text:
England have been dealt an injury blow ahead of the Nations Championship, with Guy Pepper ruled out of the upcoming fixtures.

The Bath back row suffered an ankle injury during last weekend's Gallagher PREM defeat to Gloucester at Kingsholm, forcing him off the pitch.

Bath confirmed in an injury update that Pepper will miss England's matches against Australia, Japan and New Zealand.

Steve Borthwick's side will then return to home soil for the Nations Championship finals weekend. Their opponents will depend on their final position in the northern hemisphere standings.

Pepper had already been listed as completing rehabilitation in England's squad announcement for their three-day training camp, which concludes today.

The 23-year-old began his professional career with Newcastle Falcons in 2021, scoring three tries in his first seven appearances.

His performances earned him a nomination for Premiership Rugby Breakthrough Player of the Season in 2024.

He moved to Bath ahead of the 2024/25 campaign, scoring on his league debut before playing a key role in their Premiership title-winning season. Pepper was named Man of the Match in the 2025 final.

After progressing through England's age-grade sides, he made his senior international debut as a replacement against Argentina in 2025. He scored his first England try against Fiji in July 2026.

Pepper has since established himself as an important part of Borthwick's plans.

He featured in all five matches of the Six Nations, starting four, before starting two of England's three summer Nations Championship fixtures and coming off the bench in the other.

His absence leaves England without a key back-row option and could force Borthwick to reconsider his selection ahead of the tournament.

Bath have also confirmed that Santiago Carreras has suffered a ruptured anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), ruling him out for the remainder of the season.

Dan du Preez remains unavailable for selection, although there is more encouraging news elsewhere in the squad.

Will Muir, Henry Arundell and Tom de Glanville have all returned to team training, while Thompson Cowan and Billy Sela are expected to return in the coming weeks.

England back row Sam Underhill is targeting a return in early December, while Jamie Bhatti continues to work towards making his comeback in the New Year.

title: Tadhg Furlong faces possible four-year ban
article_text:
Ireland star Tadhg Furlong could face a ban of up to four years after being cited following Leinster's clash with Munster.

The 33-year-old prop is accused of grabbing Munster star Gavin Coombes by the genitals.

The alleged act took place during Leinster's 24-18 win on Saturday.

As RUCK reported earlier, Furlong was cited on Monday.

He now faces a hearing that could lead to a lengthy ban.

Under World Rugby rules, the most severe cases can lead to a 208-week ban. That is four years.

World Rugby has strict rules on foul play.

Furlong has been cited under Law 9.27, which deals with acts against fair play.

The rules cover players who grab, twist or squeeze an opponent's genitals.

Under World Rugby's rules, the bans start at 12 weeks.

A panel will decide how serious the act was if it finds Furlong guilty.

It can also cut the ban if there are reasons to do so.

The four-year ban is the worst-case outcome.

The allegation arose during the first half of Saturday's United Rugby Championship derby.

Coombes complained to referee Andrew Brace that Tadhg Furlong had grabbed him in the groin area during a ruck.

The incident was referred to television match official Colin Stanley, but the available footage did not establish what had happened.

However, the complaint was recorded in the referee's report and later reviewed by the citing commissioner.

The URC subsequently confirmed that Furlong had been cited, with disciplinary arrangements being made.

The news comes at a bad time for Ireland.

Tadhg Furlong is still a key part of their pack.

Even a 12-week ban could rule him out of the November Tests.

A longer ban would also hit Leinster's plans and could put his place in the 2027 Six Nations at risk.

The case comes after South Africa hooker Jan-Hendrik Wessels received a nine-week ban in 2025 for a similar act.

For now, Ireland must wait for the hearing.

Furlong has yet to be found guilty, and no ban has been handed down.

title: LIV Golf’s collapse leaves the DP World Tour facing a promise it can’t afford to keep
article_text:
In the moment his week went without a headline. Charles Howell III finished his 54-hole trek around the Old Course, Carnoustie and Kingsbarns one shot on the wrong side of the cut line at the Alfred Dunhill Links earlier this month. No offense to Howell, who has put together a good career, but at 47 his results stopped being notable long ago. Except that performance is newsworthy now, because it appears those rounds were an audition. And that he’s being considered at all has irritated DP World Tour regulars, hinting at a larger mess. LIV Golf has imploded, and the European circuit must sift through the debris without cutting itself.

Interestingly, it is rubble the DP World Tour helped cause. While LIV has had too many self-inflicted wounds to list, what hindsight might consider the nascent league's knockout blow came from the DP World Tour CEO Guy Kinnings when he announced his league would no longer grant conditional releases to LIV players next year. “Players need to make a choice,” Kinnings told the BBC. “We have rules and regulations which are there to protect our tour and which our members must all abide by. Players who are not willing to comply with our rules and regulations should not be seeking to join our tour.” LIV golfers could no longer double-dip, and European players like Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton would lose Ryder Cup eligibility if they did not side with the DP World Tour. In turn, the bulk of LIV’s already-thin roster of formidable players have since signaled their intention to leave.

The old-world circuit’s move was partially defensive. Despite LIV Golf CEO Scott O’Neil saying his league wanted to “complete, not compete” the professional golf landscape, LIV had scrambled to poach DP World Tour events and sponsors for its next iteration, and that was after raiding the DP World Tour’s roster since 2022. Enough was enough. There was an upside to this calculus, too. The PGA Tour has no appetite to lift its LIV suspensions, which leaves those players desperately searching for a landing spot. A half-dozen of them would bolster DPWT fields depleted in the last few seasons by the LIV exodus along with the tour’s best players graduating to the PGA Tour.

Frankly, the DP World Tour needs the help. The tour’s 2025 numbers show a pre-tax profit of a little more than $4 million. Beneath it runs an operating loss of $85 million, sheltered by the PGA Tour helping with roughly $77 million in cash. Worse, the DP World Tour’s media-rights deal plummeted. The PGA Tour owns 30 percent of European Tour Productions, with a clause at the end of 2027 that lets the PGA Tour hand those shares back or allow the DP World Tour to buy them.

Meaning, the DP World Tour is struggling to pay its bills, and the entity helping them cover its costs could be out of the arrangement in 14 months.

Stars sell broadcast rights and sponsorships, and the DP World Tour has few of them to spare. Rahm, Hatton and Bryson DeChambeau in a field during the lean summer months are worth real money to a tour that can no longer assume someone else will cover the shortfall. The strategic alliance between the PGA Tour and DP World Tour is strong, and Kinnings (below) and new PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp have a good rapport. But does a post-LIV world challenge that relationship?

LIV’s Lee Westwood, who since settling his fines with the DP World Tour has appointed himself its civics teacher, wrote on social media that anyone who believes the PGA Tour is a DP World Tour partner instead of a rival is “either blind or fools.” Westy has been a bad-faith actor on many of golf’s issues during the schism he helped instigate. On this front, though, he has a point. Partners don’t usually come with exit clauses. If the PGA Tour can walk away from its stake next year, the DP World Tour has every reason to build a product that can stand without it, and the quickest way to do that runs through the players the PGA Tour still won’t let back in.

However, the bill for all this lands on those who stayed. Since a number of LIV players don’t have DP World Tour status, they will need sponsor’s invitations, and word among members and agents is the tour may offer 10-plus exemptions to certain LIV players. Understandably, this has not gone over well with those already on the DP World Tour, who risk getting squeezed out should LIV players get those invites. Joost Luiten said that LIV players “didn’t give a s***” about the DP World Tour when they left, and that they should have to go to Q-School. Ewen Ferguson found it comical that those who spent golf’s civil war torching the establishment act like they are coming home. Richard Mansell agreed, although he said that some should be allowed back and others should not. Basically, the rank-and-file want to know why is their tour turning from the men who stayed loyal to welcome back those who didn’t mind burning it down?

"As someone who has gone through the wringer this game provides (mostly due to my own shortcomings of course) in recent years, and who has gone back to Q School and had two immensely divergent experiences, betrayal feels like the right word," wrote DP World Tour player Eddie Pepperell in a thoughtful piece over the weekend. "And unfortunately when one feels that way inevitably what follows is a loss of respect, and what tends to fill the void left behind is resentment and contempt."

title: LIV Golf Remains 'On Track' For New Era After Announcing Key Hire
article_text:
The LIV Golf League says it remains "on track" to secure the support needed to reach its new era after appointing former TaylorMade CEO Mark King as Senior Advisor.

King spent 34 years at TaylorMade and helped to elevate the equipment manufacturers into a billion-dollar corporation before departing in 2014.

The University of Wisconsin - Green Bay alumnus also went on to spend time as president of Adidas North America and as the CEO of Taco Bell but may now face his biggest challenge in attempting to lift LIV 2.0 off the ground.

After securing an initial investment agreement from BC Partners, LIV has tried to retain as many of its 2026 playing roster as possible for the new-look league.

However, at least a dozen pros have confirmed they will not be signing up while just five have publicly committed to sticking around. A further 15 are said to also be "tentatively" in, though it is not currently known who they are.

Despite clear concerns over the viability of LIV 2.0 without the likes of Jon Rahm, Tyrrell Hatton and possibly Joaquin Niemann, the league argues it "has continued to achieve critical milestones in the process" of completing a successful recapitalization transaction which will allow its new era to take place.

One of those key milestones is the appointment of King, who will recruit, build and serve as chairman of LIV Golf's advisory board.

Commenting on the appointment, LIV Golf CEO Scott O'Neil said: "Mark is a proven leader with an extraordinary track record of transforming businesses, building iconic brands, and creating community.

"His deep understanding and relationships in and around the professional golf industry, combined with his expertise in driving innovation and building high-performing organizations, makes him a valuable addition as an advisor to our team at this pivotal moment.

"Mark's perspective and guidance will further enhance our leadership team as we build a sustainable, player-focused global tour."

King - who was reportedly touted as a potential replacement for Greg Norman back in 2022 - also spoke of his optimism over LIV's future and believes the competition of another elite-level tour can only benefit men's pro golf.

He said: "Having spent much of my career in golf, I believe there is a tremendous opportunity for LIV Golf to establish itself as a competitive and enduring force in the game.

"Competition drives innovation, creates opportunities, and ultimately makes the entire ecosystem stronger.

"The team at LIV Golf has already demonstrated its ability to attract world-class talent, break attendance records on multiple continents, engage fans across five continents, and deliver a differentiated experience.

"With a renewed business model that puts players at the center, I see significant potential for the league to build on that foundation, and create lasting value for players, fans, and partners alike."

In addition, partner and head of BC Partners Credit Ted Goldthorpe stated King's appointment is "another important step forward" as those invested carry on planning for the next iteration of LIV Golf.

Goldthorpe finished by saying the creditors "remain confident in the progress being made" towards completing a successful deal as well as "the opportunity to establish a strong foundation for LIV Golf's long-term success."

Per Flushing It on X, "the PIF have set a deadline of 30th October 2026 to determine whether they will allow BC Partners to continue the restructuring, or move towards formal liquidation."

title: David Law calls for 'change' to DP World Tour schedule over mental health concern
article_text:
David Law believes the latter part of the regular DP World Tour season “needs to change” after feeling that players battling it out for various reasons are being left exhausted.

The Aberdonian just held on to his Category 10 card after playing 11 weeks in a row, a marathon stretch that started in Denmark in mid-August and ended in Korea last week.

American Sean Crocker, who claimed the final Category 10 card after the Genesis Championship on Sunday, did likewise and spoke about how he’d been away from home for 12 weeks in total.

“The one thing I feel is that the schedule needs to change a little bit on the tour,” Law, delighted to have joined Calum Hill, Grant Forrest, Ewen Ferguson, Bob MacIntyre, Scott Jamieson and Connor Syme in securing his full status for the 2027 campaign, told The Scotsman.

“I think having 11 weeks in a row at the end of the year when you have guys fighting for jobs, guys fighting for PGA Tour cards and guys fighting to get into the Play-Offs is a bit much.

“I think finishing the season off after we’ve been in Europe for so long to go out to India and Korea with the time difference and have those as the last two counting events is pretty poor, to be honest.

“I just feel it’s not fair on guys in the situation I found myself in to be expected to play that much, especially with the uncertainty of those entry lists, which were staying so high for so long.”

While Law is looking forward to spending four weeks at home before starting the new campaign in Australia at the end of next month, players who fell short in the card battle are now set to be involved in this week’s Second Stage of the DP World Tour Qualifying School in Spain.

“I’m absolutely done in, both physically and mentally,” declared Law, who played in 30 events during the year, with only a handful of players having teed up more than the 35-year-old. “If I didn’t keep my card and had to go to the Q School next week, I don’t think I’d have any chance of competing, to be honest, and I know there are 20-30 guys who are in the exact same boat as me.

“Mental health and well being and stuff like that is spoken about a lot these days and I don’t think that last closing stretch is fair on the players and I think something needs to change.”

Next year’s schedule has already been announced - the final regular event will still be in the Far East, though a trip to Hong Kong rather than Korea - but changes could be afoot in 2028.

“Next season, I have a huge motivation to make sure I am not in the same position again and, hopefully, this time next year I am gearing up for going to the Middle East rather than trying to keep my card,” said Law, the 2019 ISPS HANDA Vic Open winner.

This season, Law played in two Rolex Series events - the Hero Dubai Desert Classic and the BMW PGA Championship - but missed out on the Genesis Scottish Open. However, he added: "Finishing in the top 100 makes a big difference in terms of scheduling and playing in the bigger events next year."

Media rights squeeze, US investment and AI tech: The sports business trends from Sportel 2026
article_text:
Now in its 36th edition, the annual Sportel conference in Monaco is one of the fixtures of the sports business calendar. It remains an incredibly important forum for media rights but is now a major event for sports technology, as well as a platform for new and existing properties to connect and share their latest updates.

At this year’s event, we heard LaLiga president Javier Tebas share his views on soccer governance and Manchester City, Mediapro explain their decision to rebrand, and The Overlap discuss their rise to become one of the most influential content platforms in soccer.

There were plenty of storylines and trends across the three days, with five that stood out in particular.

The changing dynamics of the sports media market have been apparent for some time. Streaming has allowed broadcasters to become much more data oriented in terms of how they acquire rights, leading them to prioritise big ticket properties that drive customer acquisition and retention as well as benefit from huge live audiences that deliver advertising revenue.

This has benefited the likes of the National Football League (NFL), National Basketball Association (NBA) and the Premier League, who have secured significant increases in the value of their deals. However, as they take a greater proportion of broadcasters’ budgets for sports rights, others are scrambling for a smaller piece of the pie – leading to stagnant or even contracting media revenues.

At Sportel, multiple speakers said that although media rights would continue to provide income for properties who are capable of commanding such fees, they would need to find alternative sources of revenue moving forward.

“I think properties are seeing that you cannot depend entirely on your [media] deal to drive your property,” said Hillary Mandel, EVP and head of Americas, rights at IMG. “The dollars are incredibly important, but the ecosystem that sits around that… you’ve got to own it yourself.”

Jeff Roth, founding partner at Bruin Capital added: “I agree with the middle squeeze, and if you’re in that middle, it just becomes more important to focus on match day, sponsorship, streaming, kind of businesses that we invest in… it’s even more important for the folks that cannot rely on doubling your media rights every seven years when you go to market.”

“This is not the United we knew!” 😬 How far away are Manchester United from the standards Roy once knew? 🔴 https://t.co/ZmUi8ikJIv

YouTube had a significant presence in Monaco, sharing the stage with The Overlap, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) and LiveMode across the two days. The consensus was that although live rights remained the lifeblood of sports media, content creators were helping to drive engagement and revenues across the industry.

“Live is the most important thing. Live drives everything,” explained Scott Melvin, The Overlap’s chief executive. “Rights, whilst they are king, are becoming prohibitively expensive… Very few creators, if any, will ever be able to afford Premier League rights. So, the opportunity is owning… If you can’t own the rights, own the conversation, and be 24/7.”

Pedro Pina, vice president, YouTube EMEA agreed, noting that 80 per cent of World Cup content viewership on YouTube took place in between matches.

“[Fans] love to know what happened in between matches, they want to comment, [and] they want to have a conversation by their own influencers and by their own creators,” he added, warning that rights holders and broadcasters that didn’t embrace this trend would face a potential value leak as younger viewers simply bypass official channels.

“It’s not about creators. It’s about viewers… it’s very, very difficult and very unsustainable to force viewers to have a behaviour that they don’t want to have… Water finds its way, and viewership is the same thing.

One way many rights holders are reacting to both the demand for such content and stagnating media rights values is through non-exclusive deals with creator-led channels that serve specific audiences.

The Overlap is one of several creators to be awarded Bundesliga soccer rights, while LiveMode is building on the success of sublicensing World Cup games from ESPN in Brazil by streaming selected Premier League and Champions League for free on its YouTube channel in Portugal.

“When [we] started in [Portugal], I think everyone in the industry was very concerned about our entry, with the mindset of a zero-sum game,” explained Thiago Tourinho, parter at LiveMode. “I think after the World Cup, everyone realised that it’s complementary, and we can add audiences… So after the World Cup, we did a deal with DAZN in which we have one match of the Uefa Champions League, one match of the [Premier League] every round. We are able to increase the revenue of DAZN and of [us] as well.”

“They have all the matches. They still have all the matches. Our match is not exclusive, so they also have it… So overall, we are increasing the revenue pool.”

Could AI be what immersive sport has been missing?

Five years ago, the metaverse was all the rage, fuelled by Facebook’s multi-billion-dollar rebrand as Meta and the enthusiasm of crypto advocates who believed we would all exist in a Web 3.0-enabled universe with transportable identities and digital items. Yet despite significant resources committed to creating a hardware ecosystem, building digital environments, and creating immersive applications, it’s fair to say that specific vision has not been fulfilled.

Yet proponents of immersive sporting experiences remain convinced there is a market for services that take fans closer to the action, encouraged by advances in local processing power, more desirable devices such as smart glasses, and increasing consumer appetite.

title: France refuse to give up hope of New Zealand win despite second heavy defeat
article_text:
Inexperienced France could still head home from New Zealand in early November with a win under their belts, tour captain Alexandra Chambon has insisted, despite a second comfortable defeat in seven days.

“We still finished about 20 points behind, so it’s frustrating,” she said after Saturday’s 31-12 loss at Whangarei. “We had trouble imposing our rhythm, with rucks being slowed down. Creating gaps isn’t as easy.

“They also put a lot of defensive pressure on us. If you don’t have the necessary depth or misread the situation, you get tackled – and that leads to errors. All of that held us back from playing our game effectively.”

But, she insisted, winning in Christchurch on Saturday, wasn’t so much a ‘pipe dream’ as genuine ambition. The question is whether that’s true, or just talk.

Saturday’s defeat was, undoubtedly, much better than the 13-try 81-12 hammering France had endured in Hamilton a week earlier. But it was still a sizable loss, for all that the final scores only tell part of the story.

There was a point, late in the third quarter at Semenoff Stadium, when – with the score at 14-12 – France, playing more pragmatic rugby, could have taken the lead for the third time in the match. They had New Zealand pinned deep in their own half, and were asking serious and probing questions of their defence.

“The gameplan was to avoid playing too much in our own half, to avoid exposing ourselves given the power balance, and to be more effective with our kicking,” Ratier said. “Overall, we managed to keep them pinned in their own half.

“We know they’re a team that plays a lot of attacking rugby, so they tried things. They got a bit carried away at times, and we rattled them.”

Loosehead Ambre Mwayembe, returning from suspension following her red card in the extraordinary match against Australia in Provence in September, crashed through the Black Ferns’ defensive line under the posts.

She could not ground the ball, however. Goalline dropout. New Zealand cleared and France never got as close to scoring again.

Psychologically, that was the turning point – 13 minutes later, following a devastating five-minute three-try spell of unadulterated Black Fernsness, France found themselves 31-12 down.

Head coach François Ratier recognised as much. It would be hard not to. “After [Mwayembe’s try was disallowed], we should have been incredibly tenacious because we knew how deep their bench was,” he said. “We knew that we’d have to weather the storm when they brought those players on.

“We should have been ahead at that moment. It bothers me when we get in situations we can win, like today, and we don’t.”

The numbers show France entered New Zealand’s 22 no fewer than 10 times, scoring two tries on Saturday. The Black Ferns, on the other hand, scored five tries in 11 visits to France’s 22.

In Hamilton, the week previously, New Zealand had crossed the tryline 13 times in 20 visits.

That’s France’s main problem. “The last 15 minutes [in Whang?rei] were a bit of a struggle,” Ratier understated. “They don’t necessarily reflect the game as a whole, but the [final] score is a fact.

“From the inside, we’re in a better position to analyse what happened, bounce back, and prepare for next weekend [in Christchurch] than we were last week, when we had to scrape by. This time, we’ve got something to work with.”

He’s not wrong. But for those five minutes, France were a match for New Zealand, as they had been for much of their earlier meeting in Lyon in September, their first outing since the 2026 Guinness Women’s Six Nations’ decider.

“Improved – that’s the word,” Ratier said. “We were more composed, we were able to go forward and put some things together, so that’s obviously an improvement.

“In terms of strategy, we showed we can be composed and more consistent. Now we need to finish our opportunities and make sure we score when those opportunities come — so we can keep the game really close.

“At the end, we had 14 players on the field, following an injury to another player. The last two tries were a bit heavy, but that’s the game. What’s interesting is how we performed up until the 70th minute. That’s what we’re going to work on.”

Backrow Axelle Berthoumieu and starting centres Teani Feleu and Gabrielle Vernier were all subbed off with shoulder injuries on Saturday. The latter may be fit to play in Christchurch, but early indications were not so promising for two of Les Bleues’ big ball carriers.

Mouna Touré and Cloé Correa, meanwhile, were replaced because of head injuries.

France were already nursing a long player absentee list when they headed to New Zealand – lock Siobhan Soqeta, prop Yllana Brosseau, and back-row Charlotte Escudero all joined Les Bleues’ injury lists during the matches in Lyon, Aix and La Rochelle, while Madoussou Fall Raclot is pregnant, France’s usual captain Manae Feleu is studying for medical exams, and September’s captain Pauline Bourdon Sansus stayed at home for family reasons.

This is far from a full-strength France. “We’re a very young team,” Ratier said. “We want to use this [WXV Global Series], especially here in New Zealand, to bring some new blood into the team and see how we react and how we play under massive pressure. Today, the young players responded really well,” Ratier said.

title: Report: China’s CCTV drops LaLiga coverage over Mbappe comments
article_text:
CCTV, the Chinese state broadcaster, has suspended its coverage of Spanish soccer's top-tier LaLiga, due to social media videos involving Kylian Mbappe, the Real Madrid and France superstar.

Various Chinese media outlets have reported that CCTV has taken this decision following a comment made by Mbappe in a recent interview, in which he referred to former Chinese national leader and icon Mao Zedong as a "dictator."

Mbappe had been questioned about his favorite meme, and responded by mentioning an internet picture in which his face is placed onto a portrait of Mao.

Specifically, Mbappe – who has now also been dropped by several prominent Chinese brands – said: "The [meme] that made me laugh the most is the one where they put my face on a Chinese dictator."

CCTV, it has been reported, will also not be broadcasting any fixtures involving Mbappe – for example, in the pan-European UEFA Champions League – for the moment.

Satire involving depictions of former Chinese Communist Party leaders and figures can form a punishable offence in China, due to laws which prohibit "defamation of heroes and martyrs."

Mao died in 1976, and any jokes about the former leader are seen in China as a social taboo.

CCTV (owned by China Media Group) had snapped up LaLiga rights for the ongoing 2026-27 season in mid-August, with the tie-up covering both free-to-air and pay-TV rights.

The league is also covered in China by major digital streaming platform Migu, through a four-campaign tie-up.

It has also had a physical office in Shanghai since 2014 – and Mbappe is seen as its most recognizable face.

Meanwhile, two major Chinese brands have ended their association with Mbappe over the incident: drinks heavyweight Dongpeng and dairy conglomerate Mengniu.

Mengniu, in a statement, said: "With immediate effect our company is terminating all cooperation with Kylian Mbappe. Mengniu firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people."

Dongpeng stated that it has the same approach towards "any behaviour that offends national sentiments."

In terms of recent criticism of Spanish soccer by China over similar incidents, last month, Chinese state media said that Real Madrid's messages of support to Tibet and Nepal following mass flooding in those regions featured "incorrect" wording.

In April, meanwhile, fellow LaLiga giants Barcelona apologised after a flag of disputed island Taiwan appeared on an online site linked to its international academy.

title: Coventry City signs Molson Coors beer partnership

title: Chelsea FC signs multi-year AI coaching partnership with Personar
article_text:
Chelsea FC has agreed a multi-year partnership with sports technology company Personar to expand the use of its CoachScribe platform across the club’s academy coaching operations.

The agreement builds on Chelsea’s existing relationship with the company, with the London club having been the first to adopt CoachScribe, a technology designed to capture coaching interactions and generate insights to support player and coach development.

Under the partnership, Personar will work directly with Chelsea’s academy staff to develop the platform around their coaching requirements, helping coaches review sessions and identify opportunities to improve their work with young players.

CoachScribe is designed to record and analyse coaching activity without adding to staff workloads, providing a consistent record that can be incorporated into Chelsea’s existing planning and review processes.

Sam Page, head of player and coach development at Chelsea FC, said, “Effective reflection is an integral mechanism that supports optimal learning for both players and coaches. In line with our ‘Academy Football Development BluePrint’ we want to ensure our coaches have access to insights that will enable them to optimise players’ learning. We’re pleased to be partnering with Personar, as CoachScribe will give our staff a reliable and consistent record of their coaching practice, which fits naturally into our plan-do-review process.”

The partnership forms part of Chelsea’s approach to integrating technology into its academy, with a focus on providing coaching staff with practical information that supports player development.

Jamie Sellers, Head of Football Insights and Intelligence at Chelsea FC, said, “We take a deliberate approach to the technology we introduce into the club, ensuring every solution delivers genuine value to our staff and players. CoachScribe seamlessly captures key detail and insights without adding to coaches’ workloads. By handling the analysis process efficiently, it allows our coaching staff to focus their time and energy on what matters most – coaching and developing players. We are excited about the future of this partnership and its continued evolution over the coming seasons”.

For Personar, the agreement establishes a longer-term development relationship with Chelsea as the company makes CoachScribe available to coaches at different levels of the game through the App Store and its direct sales channels.

Adrian Jones, CEO and Co-Founder of Personar, said, “We’re genuinely excited to be partnering with Chelsea Football Club on such a significant multi-year deal. Chelsea sets the standard for coaching and player development, and working alongside their staff to help the team keep excelling is exactly what CoachScribe was built for. Having a club of this calibre as a partner, not just a customer, is a huge moment for us.”

Personar was the Fan Engagement Partner at the 2026 SIAs which was won by Style Of Our Own. Alongside Mastercard, the organisations transformed women’s sport fandom into a living community through Style Of Our Own (SOOO) a new women-first sports store and cultural hub on London’s Regent Street.

title: Wales call up in-form Page after Dyer injury blow
article_text:
Dragons wing Rio Dyer has been released from the Wales squad for the Nations Championship because of a hamstring injury, with uncapped Scarlets back Mac Page called up.

Dyer was recalled by head coach Steve Tandy after a strong start to the season, but suffered an injury in the process of scoring against Ospreys last weekend.

The 26-year-old faces a spell on the sidelines and has been released to rehabilitate with the Rodney Parade club.

Dyer won the most recent of his 24 caps against South Africa last autumn and missed out on the Six Nations and summer squads.

His misfortune opens the door for uncapped Page, who is called up despite a head injury suffered for Scarlets at Stormers last Saturday.

Page scored his fifth try of the season in Cape Town but then hit his head heavily on the ground when attempting to get his sixth.

The 21-year-old was given oxygen as he was helped from the field and will go through the return-to-play protocols before pushing for a first cap.

He joins Scarlets team-mates Ellis Mee and Blair Murray as an option in the back three along with Louis Rees-Zammit, Tom Rogers, Josh Adams and Gabriel Hamer-Webb.

Page, who can also play at outside centre, was a member of Wales' touring party to Japan in 2025 but did not feature.

Wales play Japan in Cardiff on Saturday, 7 November and then host New Zealand and Australia.

Tandy's side then take on another southern hemisphere opponent on Nations Championship finals weekend at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium at the end of the month.

title: Jacob Fearnley retires hurt against Arthur Fery at Vienna Open as Harriet Dart extends winning run
article_text:
Jacob Fearnley retired with an injury after losing 5-1 in the first set against Arthur Fery to give his fellow countryman a place in the second round at the Vienna Open.

Fearnley was broken by Fery in just his second service game, with the British No 1 winning the next two games on the bounce and looking set to consign his opponent to a comprehensive first-set loss.

Fearnley, though, then put a stop to the contest, shaking the umpire's hand and retiring with an unspecified injury, allowing Fery safe passage to the next stage of the competition.

Fery will face the winner of No 6 seed Francis Tiafoe and Lorenzo Musetti - the latter of whom he lost against in straight sets at the US Open - in the second round.

Harriet Dart maintained her winning form at the Guangzhou Open in China as she beat Russian qualifier Tatiana Prozorova 6-4 2-6 6-2 to reach the second round.

Dart, who also came through two qualifiers, will next face Uzbekistan's Polina Kudermetova or Indonesia's Janice Tjen in the last 16 after winning a see-saw battle against world number 123 Prozorova.

Both players struggled to hold serve, but the British number five broke three times in the decider to open up a 5-2 lead and served out to seal victory in two hours and 15 minutes.

British teenager Mika Stojsavljevic slipped to a heavy first-round defeat at the Toray Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo, losing 6-1 6-2 to Filipino world number 19 Alexandra Eala in one hour and 15 minutes.

Stojsavljevic, 17, who won the girls' US Open singles title at the 2024 US Open, was broken twice in both sets by the world number 19 after being given a wildcard into the WTA 500 tournament.

title: PGA Tour star agreed secret LIV Golf deal before career-defining U-turn
article_text:
Life is full of sliding doors moments. A few of those, in the money-crazed bubble of golf at least, came in the summer of 2022 shortly after the civil war that would rip the sport apart ignited.

A number of stars, some rising and others fading, had to decide whether to accept unimaginable riches and join the controversial Saudi-backed LIV Golf Invitational, as it was known then, or relent and remain with the PGA Tour. Four years on, those decisions have had lasting impacts upon careers and – to a lesser extent – legacies.

However, it is impossible to predict just how consequential a move to LIV would have been to the career trajectory of one of the very best players in the world.

At the time, LIV’s interest in Cam Young was well known.

His breakthrough year in 2022 had included top five finishes at both the PGA Championship and The Open. A PGA Tour win was surely around the corner.

But Young was seriously interested in ditching the PGA Tour for LIV, and it has been revealed in recent bankruptcy filings just how close the American was to crossing the divide.

The filings show that four years ago, Young signed an “intent-to-play” agreement with LIV which would have made him one of the biggest coups for then CEO Greg Norman before LIV’s second season.

“Frankly, I have decided to stay,” Young eventually confirmed at the 2022 Tour Championship. “So, I don’t know, it’s a really difficult situation because it’s not really anything anyone wanted to happen.

“I think it wasn’t meant to be this hostile between the two. Frankly, throughout the whole process with [LIV], I was very interested. I think they have a bunch of good ideas and are doing some cool stuff.

“With some of the changes coming [to the PGA Tour], that’s kind of what really helped me decide to kind of stay and pursue those goals that I have for myself, like making a Presidents Cup team and a Ryder Cup team and winning a major when all of that is just uncertain if you go. It’s a tough place for me because, you know, I’m very young and there are a lot of factors.”

Young does not have a major in his locker yet and his career did not in kickstart in 2023. In fact, his struggle to win a PGA Tour title remained a desperate storyline for another couple of seasons.

But Young is now a bona fide star. He is ranked fourth in the world, the current Players champion, and he has played pivotal roles on Presidents Cup and Ryder Cup teams, just like he had dreamed.

LIV has proved less fertile ground for emerging stars in recent years, owing to the league’s struggle to secure world ranking points and therefore clear pathways into the majors. When Young signed his initial agreement – dated July 24, 2022, exactly a week after his runner-up finish in the Open at St Andrews – he knew he was preparing to take a big leap of faith.

And perhaps Young was always destined to reside among the very elite regardless.

But he will also feel vindicated that he trusted his instincts with a change of heart that has indisputably altered the course of his career.

title: Charlotte FC, Ally agree to extend front-of-kit sponsorship into 2030s
article_text:
Ally Financial will remain Charlotte FC’s front-of-kit sponsor well into the next decade after extending a partnership that dates to the MLS club’s inaugural season in 2022. The sides reached the agreement with multiple seasons remaining on the current deal, in part to account for MLS’s move to a summer-to-spring calendar next year.

Financial terms and the precise duration of the extension were not disclosed. The Charlotte Business Journal reported the bank is paying an average of $8M per year under the current deal. MLS front-of-kit sponsorships are typically valued in the mid-seven-figure range annually, with SponsorUnited estimating the average this season at $5.1M.

In addition to being Charlotte FC’s most lucrative sponsorship, Ally Chief Marketing and PR Officer Andrea Brimmer said it is one of the bank’s largest investments when considering “sponsorship fees, as well as the activation.”

“One thing about Ally that makes this so rewarding is how heavily involved they are in activation and engagement,” said Tepper Sports & Entertainment CRO Eric Sudol. “Andrea and her team understand what the definition of success is. We know the KPIs and the bogeys that we’re up against. So, if you’re hitting those along the way, then by all means you continue.”

The sponsorship package will largely remain the same, with the front-of-kit placement serving as the core asset. Ally will continue to sponsor the Pitches for Progress community initiative through which the partners have opened seven mini-pitches in at-risk communities. The brand’s logo is also displayed in the center circle during team entrances before each match.

“We had over 500 Ally employees that have had an opportunity to volunteer through the partnership, which we really like,” Brimmer said. “And then, just the ability to have everything from the media to the in-stadium signage to the rights to use the logo and the marks, especially with a really hot soccer calendar. So, all of those things persist. It’s been a pretty robust deal. We’re really doubling down on the things that we’ve done and just being creative with them as we go forward.”

Brimmer said the Charlotte FC deal has driven positive business results, including a 22% jump in Ally’s brand awareness among MLS fans. The Detroit-based digital financial services firm maintains its largest employment hub in Uptown Charlotte, and Brimmer said the MLS club partnership has helped attract and retain talent. The bank also soft-launched its new customer loyalty program, Loyally, with Charlotte FC fans this season before rolling it out nationwide.

One unusual wrinkle of the relationship between Charlotte FC and Ally is that the team plays in a stadium named for Bank of America, a competitor to Ally in financial services. Tepper Sports & Entertainment, which owns both Charlotte FC and the Carolina Panthers, signed a long-term extension of its naming-rights agreement with Bank of America earlier this year.

That agreement limits the stadium-specific assets TS&E can offer Ally, including naming rights to premium spaces, but the two financial institutions have worked to ensure their sponsorship assets do not conflict.

“It is unique, but we’ve had a lot of direct conversation with the leadership at Bank of America and just worked through it so that we both can protect our assets and protect our investment, but do it in a way that doesn’t compete with one another,” Brimmer said.

The Ally extension comes as Bank of America Stadium and its surrounding campus undergo a $1.3B transformation. Sudol said TS&E is in the market with sponsorship inventory tied to new premium spaces and expects the renovated facility to have at least eight “cornerstone” partners (in addition to Bank of America) when it opens by the start of the 2030 MLS and NFL seasons.

title: Wales star ruled out of autumn series as Steve Tandy calls up exciting replacement
article_text:
Uncapped wing Macs Page has been called up to Wales' squad for the Nations Championship, with Rio Dyer ruled out of the autumn due to injury.

The Scarlets youngster was one of the notable absentees from Steve Tandy's autumn squad last week, having started the season in fine form for the west Walians.

Having crossed for four tries in his first four matches of the season, Page had been expected to feature in Wales' squad - having previously been called up once before for the tour of Japan last year.

However, the 21-year-old was ultimately not included.

Instead, Tandy opted for Josh Adams, Gabriel Hamer-Webb, Ellis Mee, Blair Murray, Louis Rees-Zammit, Tom Rogers and Dyer as his back-three options.

Unfortunately, having earned a Wales recall after a year out of the squad, Dyer was forced off halfway through the Dragons' defeat to Ospreys on Saturday night - having just scored.

Page was also forced off injured on the weekend, having suffered a head injury after trying to score his second try against the Stormers.

The Scarlets confirmed on Monday that Page would fly home from South Africa, as he wasn't fit to face the Bulls this weekend.

“Macs improved fairly quickly post match," said the Scarlets in a statement. "He will not be available for next weekend’s game against the Vodacom Bulls as he will follow World Rugby guidelines following a concussive injury.”

He will join Taine Plumtree and Joe Hawkins, who are also flying back from South Africa to join up with the national team.

Following his initial omission, Scarlets director of rugby Nigel Davies had said it was only a matter of time before he was brought in by Wales.

“Obviously he’s been excellent in the first block of the season. It’s great that we’ve got seven boys in there and a lot of people are saying we should have eight with Macs,” Davies said.

“I think Macs has been brilliant, what he needs to do is maintain his form really. I think from a Welsh perspective, Steve Tandy has probably got a situation where he hasn’t had before where he’s got some really tough calls in most positions now.

“We’re creating a lot of depth, which we haven’t had, so he’s got some tough calls to make.”

Davies said Page “no doubt would have been one of those tough calls”.

“What Macs has got to do is just keep on going," he added. "His form is great; he’s got to be able to maintain that now. I’m sure if he does, he’s going to come into contention again.”

“I suppose with Macs, it’s a matter of when, not if, he plays for Wales, given the way he’s developing. Definitely if he carries on the way he is. I think he’s just getting better.”

There had been rumours that Page qualified for Ireland, following links to Munster in the summer.

However, WalesOnline understands those rumours are wide of the mark.

title: Jannik Sinner set for a potential return after knee injury as Six Kings Slam rescheduled to December
article_text:
World No. 1 Jannik Sinner is set to return to action at the Six Kings Slam in Saudi Arabia in December after the lucrative exhibition tournament was postponed from its original October dates amid security concerns in the region, Reuters reported on Monday.

The Italian had announced earlier this month that he would not compete again in 2026 as he continued his recovery from a knee injury that has kept him out of action since his Wimbledon triumph in July. However, the revised schedule for the Six Kings Slam could see the two-time defending champion make a comeback before the end of the year.

The exhibition event, which was originally scheduled to take place in Riyadh from October 21 to 24, has been rescheduled for December 27 to 30.

Sinner's potential return at the Six Kings Slam comes after a period on the sidelines following his Wimbledon victory in July. The 25-year-old had indicated that he would skip the European indoor hard-court season and the ATP Finals in Turin, where he has won the title in each of the last two editions.

His participation in the rescheduled exhibition would therefore mark a significant development in his recovery, although it remains separate from his official ATP Tour commitments.

Sinner has dominated the Six Kings Slam since its introduction, beating Spanish rival Carlos Alcaraz in both finals. The Italian earned $6 million for each victory, underlining the extraordinary financial rewards on offer at the non-ATP event.

, Alexander Zverev, Taylor Fritz and Alex de Minaur. The presence of several of the sport's leading names is expected to make the December event one of the most closely watched exhibitions on the tennis calendar. With Sinner and Alcaraz having contested the previous two finals, their potential meeting in Riyadh would renew one of the biggest rivalries in men's tennis.

title: Rafael Nadal announces sensational return to the court after 'living in pain'
article_text:
Rafael Nadal has confirmed that he will retirn to the tennis court for a one-off exhibition event in Las Vegas next year. The 22-time Grand Slam champion retired from professional tennis two years ago, but has barely placed since. But he will now be back in action at the The MGM Slam inside the T-Mobile Arena on February 28. Nadal faced Carlos Alcaraz in another exhibition match in Las Vegas back in 2024, and said he was looking forward to competing there again.

The announcement of Nadal's exhibition match comes after the 40-year-old opened up on living in pain throughout his career. Since retiring, the Spanish star has chronicled his career in a Netflix documentary series, Rafa, and is now releasing a new coffee-table book with Assouline.

Both have given an insight into the extent of the injuries Nadal faced during his glittering career. Ahead of the release of his Assouline book, the former world No. 1 told The Athletic: "For me every moment was ... I always had not the fear but knew that it could be my last year on tour.

"The only positive thing I've taken from all the injuries was that I was able to enjoy more and put more value on the great moments. But I lived all my tennis career with pain - on a daily basis, I had too much pain."

Nadal has barely touched a racket in retirement, also admitting that he hasn't missed tennis too much. But after two years away from the game, he's finally ramping things up.

The 92-time title winner recently got back on court for the Rafa Nadal Academy Slam, an exhibition event celebrating a decade of his tennis centre in Mallorca. Nadal and some of his fellow retired ex-rivals contested a series of 10-point doubles tiebreaks, and his team won.

Now, Nadal is taking things up a notch with his friendly in Las Vegas. In a new video, he said: "I have great memories from 2024, playing in Les Vegas. The atmosphere and the fans were simply amazing.

"So I am very excited to announce that I will be back in 2027, and I am very looking forward again to compete in the MGM Slam, so see you soon in Vegas."

Nadal lost to Alcaraz in a match tiebreak last time out, with the younger Spaniard taking it 14-12. Although he is now retired, the 40-year-old said his love for competing had not waned.

"I remember how impressive it was to feel the energy of a full arena in a city like Las Vegas. After that match in 2024, now I return in a different stage of my life, without the pressure of the tour but with the same passion for this sport," he added.

"I have always loved competing, and even if my professional career is finished, that feeling never really goes away."
